## The question

How hard is it to forecast Italian electricity demand, and what should a model
beat before it is worth using? I started with Terna's national load series and
its own published forecast. The first result is a benchmark, not a claim that
my model beats the grid operator.

## The first measured result

I compared forecasts against **2,688 national load observations** at 15 minute
intervals from **1–28 February 2026**. All three methods are evaluated on the
same timestamps.

| Forecast | MAE (MW) | RMSE (MW) | MAPE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Terna's published forecast | **531** | **721** | **1.39%** |
| Same time one week earlier | 946 | 1,266 | 2.45% |
| Same time one day earlier | 3,319 | 5,257 | 8.89% |

Terna's forecast is substantially better than either naive baseline in this
month. The gap between the daily and weekly baselines also shows why calendar
structure matters: an ordinary weekday is often more like the same weekday last
week than like yesterday.

The comparison uses the `total_load_MW` and `forecast_total_load_MW` fields from
Terna's [Total Load API](https://developer.terna.it/docs/read/apis_catalog/load/Total_Load).
That API describes the forecast as produced the day before the reference day.
The naive forecasts use only earlier observed load. I joined each observation
to the timestamp exactly one or seven days earlier; shifting by row number
would give wrong matches wherever the extract has a gap. February has complete
15 minute coverage in this local extract.

[Read the benchmark script](benchmark.py){.more-link}

## Does the result hold beyond February?

I repeated the same comparison for every complete month from February through
May 2026: **11,520 national observations** in total. Each monthly window has
all its expected 15 minute UTC timestamps; all three forecasts are scored on
exactly the same observations.

| Month | Observations | Terna MAE (MW) | Previous week MAE (MW) | Previous day MAE (MW) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| February | 2,688 | **531** | 946 | 3,319 |
| March | 2,976 | **501** | 808 | 3,300 |
| April | 2,880 | **650** | 1,886 | 2,955 |
| May | 2,976 | **585** | 1,810 | 3,118 |
| **Pooled** | **11,520** | **567** | **1,369** | **3,171** |

Terna's published forecast has the lowest MAE in each month. The weekly naive
baseline is much less stable: its error more than doubles between March and
April. This comparison shows the change, but it does not identify its cause.
The pooled row scores all 11,520 observations together rather than averaging
the four monthly MAEs.

Run `python benchmark.py /path/to/total_load.parquet --monthly` to reproduce
this table from a Terna extract with the same fields. The script rejects an
incomplete month instead of quietly scoring the rows that happen to be present.

## The data pipeline

The broader project downloads public Terna data into a local Parquet layer. Its
catalog script supports incremental updates, handles intermittent API errors
with retries, and records which endpoint and parameter combinations return
data. The load series spans 2021–2026 and includes national and regional data.

Each record carries a local timestamp and UTC offset. I combine them before
sorting or aggregating, so the repeated hour when clocks change remains
unambiguous. The February benchmark uses UTC timestamps and stays away from a
clock change.

The coverage check also found a 48-hour gap in January 2026 in this local
extract. June is only a partial month. I excluded both from the monthly table;
otherwise a seemingly comparable score would describe a different time window.

## What is built, and what comes next

The `handcast` package contains mean and seasonal naive forecasters, error
metrics, and a chronological train/test split, with focused tests. Its
rolling-origin split and recursive forecasting methods are still
unimplemented. I am not presenting a fitted model score until those methods
support a proper out-of-sample comparison.

The expanded table covers four months and national load only. It is a benchmark
of existing forecasts and timestamp-matched naive rules, not a backtest of a
model I trained. The next useful result is a rolling backtest of a fitted model
across several origins, with Terna and the weekly naive forecast in every
comparison. Any model that uses observed weather must also be labeled
accordingly: Terna's day-ahead forecast did not have access to the next day's
observed temperature.
